title: 論語 憲問第十四
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 14, 〈憲問〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 14 of the Analects, 憲問 Xiàn wèn, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'Xian asked', Yuan Xian, the austere disciple, asking what is shameful. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. With 47 passages this is the longest book, and the most various. It judges men of the recent past — Zichan, Guan Zhong, Duke Huan of Qi, Duke Wen of Jin — and Zilu and Zigong press the Master on whether Guan Zhong, who served the man who had his own lord killed, can be called humane (14.17–14.18). Here are the gentleman ashamed to let his words outrun his deeds (14.29); the answer to 'repaying injury with virtue' — then with what do you repay virtue? (14.36); Kongzi bathing and going to court to ask that a regicide in Qi be punished (14.22); the gatekeeper's remark on the man who knows a thing is impossible and works at it all the same (14.41); and the basket-carrier who hears the Master's chime-stones and calls him stubborn (14.42). Toward the end come encounters with recluses and men who left the world, which lead on to Book 18. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
憲問恥。
子曰：「
邦有道，穀；
邦無道，穀，
恥也。」
sentences.l:
Xian asked about shame.
The Master said: “When the state has the Way — a salary;
when the state lacks the Way — a salary:
that is shameful.”
sentences.i: Xian asked what is shameful. The Master said: “To do nothing but draw an official's pay while the state is on the Way, and to go on drawing it when the state has lost the Way — both are a disgrace.”
sentences.n: The book is named 憲問 from its opening words; Zhu Xi's heading quotes Hu Yin (胡氏): this book was perhaps recorded by Yuan Xian, and it has forty-seven chapters (此篇疑原憲所記，凡四十七章). 憲 xiàn is Yuan Xian 原憲, the Yuan Si of 6.3 (Zhu Xi: 憲原思名); he is named by his personal name, as a man names himself — perhaps why Hu Yin thought the book his record. 穀 'grain' is an officer's pay, reckoned in grain (Zhu Xi: 穀禄也), as in 8.12. The two halves are bare: 'state has the Way — salary; state lacks the Way — salary', and 恥也 'shameful' sums up. Zhu Xi takes both as shameful: when the state has the Way, to be unable to do anything worth doing, and when it lacks the Way, to be unable to keep oneself good alone — knowing only how to eat one's salary — are both a disgrace. Xian, guarded and upright (狷介), surely knew already that a salary under a lawless state is shameful, but not that one under a well-ruled state can be; so the Master took his question and spoke of both, to widen his aim and spur him to do something. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the first half the other way: when the state has the Way one should eat its salary; it is taking a salary at the court of a lord without the Way that is shameful. Compare 8.13, where poverty under a well-ruled state is the shame.

sentences.t:
克、伐、怨、欲
不行焉，
可以為仁矣？
sentences.l:
The urge to win, boasting, resentment and desire
not carried out in him —
can that count as humaneness?
sentences.i: If a man keeps the urge to get the better of others, boastfulness, resentment and greed from ever showing in what he does, may that be called humaneness?
sentences.n: Yuan Xian asks again — Zhu Xi: this too is Yuan Xian asking from what he himself could do (此亦原憲以其所能而問也). The line has no speaker and no 曰, and is left unquoted. Four nouns, each a fault, then 不行焉 'are not carried out in him'. Zhu Xi: 克 is loving to win (好勝), 伐 boasting of oneself (自矜), 怨 anger and grudge (忿恨), 欲 greed (貪欲). He Yan's Ma Rong (his text writes 剋): loving to get the better of others, boasting of one's achievements, petty grudges, greed. 可以為仁 'can thereby count as humaneness', 為 wéi; 矣 states the conclusion he hopes he has reached, and the Master's reply shows it is put as a question.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
可以為難矣，
仁則吾不知也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “It can count as hard;
as for humaneness, I do not know.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “That may be called difficult. Whether it is humaneness, I cannot say.”
sentences.n: 可以為難 'can count as hard' (為 wéi, 難 nán) answers his 可以為仁 word for word, changing only the last word. 仁則吾不知也 'humaneness — then I do not know': 則 after a topic sets it against what went before, and 'I do not know' is the Master's way of withholding the name, as 5.4 and 5.7. Zhu Xi: to have these four and be able to check them so they cannot act may be called hard; but humaneness is Heaven's principle whole and undivided, free of the burden of the four of itself — 'not carried out' is not enough to speak of it. He quotes Master Cheng: to be without the four is something only the humane can do; to have them and master the feelings so they do not act is also hard to do, but to call it humaneness is not right — here the sage opened the matter deeply, and it is a pity Xian could not ask again. The comment then takes up an objection — is not keeping the four from acting the 'overcoming the self' (克己, 12.1), the way to seek humaneness? No: overcoming the self's selfishness to return to the rites leaves no selfish desire behind and recovers Heaven's principle as it is; merely to check them and not act has no thought of pulling up the root of the sickness, and lets it lie hidden in the breast. He Yan's Bao Xian: these four are hard to keep from acting, but that is not yet humaneness.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
士而懐居，
不足以為士矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “An officer who cherishes his comforts
is not fit to count as an officer.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man of service who hankers after the comforts of home does not deserve the name.”
sentences.n: 士 is the officer, the man of service, as 4.9. 而 'and yet' joins the noun to a verb phrase: 'an officer, and (yet) cherishing…'. 懐 huái, the edition's form of 懷, is 'to cherish, to hold in one's heart', as 4.11 君子懷德. 居 is more than 'home': Zhu Xi: wherever one's thoughts find ease and comfort (意所便安處也). 不足以為士 'not enough to count as an officer', 為 wéi. He Yan's comment (unnamed): an officer should set his heart on the Way and not seek ease; one who cherishes his dwelling is no officer.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
邦有道，
危言危行；
邦無道，
危行言孫。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “When the state has the Way,
lofty in speech, lofty in conduct;
when the state lacks the Way,
lofty in conduct, humble in speech.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When the state is on the Way, speak high-mindedly and act high-mindedly. When it has lost the Way, still act high-mindedly, but speak with care and deference.”
sentences.n: 危 here is not 'in peril' but 'high, steep' (Zhu Xi: 危高峻也) — words and deeds that stand tall; He Yan's Bao Xian takes it as 'stern' (厲): when the state has the Way one may be stern in word and deed. 孫 is read xùn and is the same word as 遜 'yielding, humble' (Zhu Xi: 孫卑順也); He Yan's text writes 遜. Zhu Xi marks both 行 and 孫 去聲: for 行 'conduct' that is xìng, a reading modern practice does not keep (we print xíng); for 孫 it is xùn. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun (尹氏): the gentleman's holding of himself may not change, but in speech there are times when he dares not say everything, to escape disaster — and so for one who governs a state to bring its officers to humble speech is surely perilous. The comment that follows in He Yan (unnamed): conduct stays stern and does not follow the crowd; speech yields, to keep harm far off.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
有徳者必有言，
有言者不必有徳；
仁者必有勇，
勇者不必有仁。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man of virtue will always have something worth saying, but one who has plenty to say is not always a man of virtue. The humane man will always have courage, but the brave man is not always humane.”
sentences.n: Two pairs of one shape: 有X者必有Y 'one who has X surely has Y', then the reverse with 不必 'not necessarily'. 徳 is the edition's form of 德. Zhu Xi: one who has virtue has harmony and order stored within, and its flower shows outside; one who can speak may be merely glib and quick of tongue (便佞口給). The humane have no selfish burden on the heart, and seeing what is right they will surely do it; the brave may have only the strength of blood and breath (血氣之强). He quotes Yin Tun: one with virtue surely has words, but one merely able to speak need not have virtue; the humane man's will is surely brave, but one merely brave need not have humaneness. He Yan's one comment (unnamed): virtue cannot be got at by guessing, so it must show itself in words.

sentences.t:
南宫适問於孔子曰：「
羿善射，
奡盪舟，
俱不得其死然；
禹、稷躬稼而有天下。」
夫子不答。
南宫适出。
子曰：「
君子哉若人！
尚徳哉若人！」

sentences.l:
Nangong Kuo asked Kongzi, saying: “Yi was good at archery,
Ao shoved boats along,
yet neither got his proper death;
Yu and Ji sowed grain with their own hands and came to have the world.”
The Master did not answer.
Nangong Kuo went out.
The Master said: “A gentleman indeed, this man!
One who prizes virtue indeed, this man!”
sentences.i: Nangong Kuo put it to Kongzi: “Yi was a matchless archer and Ao could drive a boat over dry land, yet neither of them died a natural death. Yu and Ji laboured in the fields with their own hands, and they came to possess the world.” The Master made no reply. When Nangong Kuo had gone out, the Master said: “There is a gentleman for you! How he honours virtue, that man!”
sentences.n: 适 is read kuò (Zhu Xi: 古活反). Zhu Xi: Nangong Kuo is Nan Rong (5.1, 11.5); He Yan's Kong Anguo calls him Nangong Jingshu (南宫敬叔), a grandee of Lu. 羿 Yì (音詣) and 奡 Ào (五報反) are figures of the remote past. Zhu Xi: Yi, lord of Youqiong (有窮), a fine archer, destroyed Xiang of the Xia and usurped his throne, and his minister Han Zhuo (寒浞) in turn killed Yi and took his place; Ao — the Chunqiu commentary writes 澆 — was Zhuo's son, so strong he could move a boat over dry land, and was later put to death by Shaokang of the Xia. 盪舟 'to shove a boat': Zhu Xi spells 盪 土浪反 (tàng); we print the modern dàng. 俱不得其死然 'both did not get their (proper) death', the phrase used of Zilu at 11.12; 然 closes the sentence. Zhu Xi: Yu levelled the waters and the land, and Ji (Lord Millet, ancestor of Zhou) sowed the grain; both did the work of farming themselves (躬稼); Yu received the throne from Shun, and Ji's descendants, down to King Wu of Zhou, also came to have the world. Kuo's meaning, Zhu Xi says, was to liken Yi and Ao to the men of power of his day and Yu and Ji to Kongzi, so Kongzi did not answer; yet one who speaks so is a man of the gentleman's kind with a heart that prizes virtue, and must not go unacknowledged, so the Master waited until he had gone out and praised him. He Yan's Ma Rong reads the silence as modesty: Kuo meant to liken Kongzi to Yu and Ji, and Kongzi, being modest, did not answer. 君子哉若人 is the cry of 5.2, the praise put first: 'a gentleman indeed — this man!'; 尚 'to prize, to put above'. Kong Anguo: he despised what was not right and valued virtue, so the Master called him a gentleman.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子而不仁者有矣夫，
未有小人而仁者也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Gentlemen who are yet not humane — there are such, ah!
There has never been a small man who was yet humane.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There have been gentlemen who fell short of humaneness, alas; but there has never been a petty man who was humane.”
sentences.n: X而Y者 'one who is X and yet Y'; 有矣夫 'there are, ah!' — 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶) is a final exclamation, a sigh. 未有…也 'there has never been…'. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo (謝氏): the gentleman has set his heart on humaneness; yet if for the space of a hair or an instant his heart is not on it, he cannot escape being not humane. He Yan's Kong Anguo: though called a gentleman, he is not yet complete.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
愛之，
能勿勞乎？
忠焉，
能勿誨乎？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Loving someone,
can one not make him toil?
Wholehearted toward him,
can one not instruct him?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Can you love a man and not make him work hard? Can you be wholehearted toward him and not set him right?”
sentences.n: Two matched questions, each 'can one not…?' expecting 'one cannot'. 之 and 焉 both point to the person loved or served: 焉 is 'toward him' (the fused 於之). 勞 láo is used as a verb, 'to make toil'; 勿 'not'. Zhu Xi quotes Su Shi (蘇氏): to love and not make toil is the love of birds and beasts for their young (禽犢之愛); to be wholehearted and not instruct is the wholeheartedness of women and eunuchs (婦寺之忠); to love and know to make him toil — that love is deep; to be wholehearted and know to instruct — that wholeheartedness is great. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads 勞 as 勞来 'to urge on and encourage': whom one loves one will surely wish to spur on, and to whom one is wholehearted one will surely wish to teach.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
為命，
裨諶草創之，
世叔討論之，
行人子羽脩飾之，
東里子産潤色之。」

Shishu — You Ji, a grandee of Zheng
the envoy — the officer for missions

sentences.l:
The Master said: “In making a dispatch,
Pi Chen drafted it in rough,
Shishu examined and discussed it,
the envoy Ziyu trimmed and dressed it,
Zichan of Dongli gave it lustre and colour.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When Zheng had a state letter to prepare, Pi Chen made the first draft, Shishu went over it and weighed every point, Ziyu, the officer for embassies, cut and added to it, and Zichan of Dongli gave it its final polish.”
sentences.n: 為命 'making a 命', a dispatch or state document — Zhu Xi: the state of Zheng's making of its diplomatic letters (鄭國之為辭命). 裨諶 is read Pí Chén (Zhu Xi: 婢之反, 時林反). All four, Zhu Xi says, were grandees of Zheng. 草 'rough' (畧), 創 chuàng 'to make' (造): to make a draft. Shishu is You Ji 游吉, written Zitaishu (子太叔) in the Chunqiu commentary. 討 'to search out' (尋究), 論 'to discuss' (講議). The 行人 is the officer in charge of missions; Ziyu is Gongsun Hui 公孫揮 (not the disciple Tantai Mieming of 6.12, who was also styled Ziyu). 脩飾 means adding and cutting. Dongli is a place, where Zichan lived; 潤色 means adding literary colour. Zheng's letters always passed through the hands of these four worthies, detailed, careful and exact, each doing what he did best, so in answering the lords they seldom came to grief; Kongzi says this in approval. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Pi Chen planned well in the countryside but not in the city, so when Zheng had business with the lords it sent him out by carriage into the country to plan the wording of covenants and meetings. Ma Rong: 討 is 'to put in order' (治); Zichan lived at Dongli and was named from it; passing through these four worthies, their letters seldom failed. Variants: He Yan's text writes 卑諶 for 裨諶, and reads 脩飾東里 with no 之 after 脩飾.

sentences.t:
或問子産。
子曰：「
惠人也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Chan (in the name 子産, 産 being the edition's form of 產)

sentences.l:
Someone asked about Zichan.
The Master said: “A kind man.”
sentences.i: Someone asked about Zichan. The Master said: “A man who was good to people.”
sentences.n: Zichan is the minister of Zheng of 5.15 and the last unit. 惠 'kind, bestowing benefits', as 5.15 其養民也惠. Zhu Xi: Zichan's government did not rest on leniency alone, but in his heart he made loving people the chief thing, so Kongzi called him a kind man, naming what weighed most in him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 惠 is love; Zichan was 'a love left over from antiquity' (古之遺愛).

sentences.t:
問子西。
曰：「
彼哉！
彼哉！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He asked about Zixi.
He said: “That one!
That one!”
sentences.i: He asked about Zixi. The Master said: “Oh, him! Him!”
sentences.n: The questioner and the speaker are understood from the unit before. 彼 bǐ 'that one'; 哉 makes it an exclamation. Zhu Xi: Zixi was Prince Shen 申 of Chu; he could decline the throne of Chu, set up King Zhao and reform the government, and he too was a worthy grandee; but he could not do away with Chu's usurped title of king, and when King Zhao wished to employ Kongzi he blocked it; later he summoned the Duke of Bai (白公) and so brought on disaster and rebellion — what kind of man he was can be known from this. 彼哉 is a phrase that puts a man outside (外之之辭). He Yan's Ma Rong: Zixi was a grandee of Zheng, and 彼哉彼哉 means he is not worth mentioning; some say he is Zixi, chief minister of Chu.

sentences.t:
問管仲。
曰：「
人也。
奪伯氏駢邑三百，
飯疏食，
没齒無怨言。」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
He asked about Guan Zhong.
He said: “This man:
he took from Bo the town of Pian, three hundred households;
Bo ate coarse rice,
and to the end of his years spoke no word of resentment.”
sentences.i: He asked about Guan Zhong. The Master said: “There was a man! He took from Bo the town of Pian with its three hundred households, and Bo lived on coarse fare to the end of his days without a word of complaint.”
sentences.n: Guan Zhong is Duke Huan of Qi's minister, of 3.22. 人也 — Zhu Xi: like saying 'this man' (此人也); He Yan's comment (unnamed) likens it to the Ode's 'the man I mean' (所謂伊人). The subject changes without being named: Guan Zhong took, Bo ate. 伯氏 Bo was a grandee of Qi, 駢邑 the place's name, 齒 'years' (Zhu Xi). 飯疏食 'ate coarse rice', 疏 shū, 食 sì, as 7.15. 没 mò 'to the end of'. Zhu Xi: presumably (葢) Duke Huan took Bo's town to give to Guan Zhong; Bo knew his own guilt and in his heart acknowledged Guan Zhong's merit, so he lived out his life in straitened means and spoke no resentment — this is the affair Xunzi means by 'he gave him three hundred shrines of the soil, and none of the rich dared refuse him'. The comment adds, for someone who asked which was the better, Guan Zhong or Zichan: Guan Zhong's virtue did not match his talent, Zichan's talent did not match his virtue; but of the sage's learning neither had heard anything. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Bo's fief was three hundred households; Guan Zhong took it and brought him to coarse fare, yet to the end of his days he spoke no resentment, because it was justly done (以當其理).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
貧而無怨難，
富而無驕易。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Poor yet without resentment — hard;
rich yet without arrogance — easy.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It is hard to be poor and bear no grudge, and easy to be rich and not be overbearing.”
sentences.n: Two matched lines, each a subject phrase (貧而無怨 'poor yet without resentment') and a one-word verdict: 難 nán 'hard', 易 yì 'easy' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 富而無驕 is the phrase of 1.15. Zhu Xi: to bear poverty well is hard and to bear wealth well is easy — that is the ordinary way of human feeling; but one should work at the hard and not neglect the easy. He Yan has no comment.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
孟公綽為趙、魏老則優，
不可以為滕、薛大夫。」

morph.gloss: Meng Gongchuo — a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Meng Gongchuo, as house elder to Zhao or Wei, would have more than enough;
he could not be grandee of Teng or Xue.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Meng Gongchuo would be more than equal to the post of chief retainer in the house of Zhao or Wei, but he could not serve as a grandee in Teng or Xue.”
sentences.n: 為 wéi 'to be, to serve as', twice. 則優 'then (he would be) ample': 優 yōu is 'having more than enough' (Zhu Xi: 有餘也). Zhu Xi: Gongchuo was a grandee of Lu. Zhao and Wei were ministerial houses of Jin, and 老 is the house elder, the chief of the house officers; a great house has weight but none of a state's business, and its house elder is honoured but has no official charge. Teng and Xue are the names of two states, and a grandee is one entrusted with a state's government; Teng and Xue were small states with much business, where a grandee's rank was high and his charge heavy. So Gongchuo, Zhu Xi concludes, was probably (葢) clean, quiet and of few desires, but short of talent. He quotes Yang Shi: not to know a man beforehand and use him against his talent is to throw him away — this is why the gentleman worries about not knowing men, and from these words one can see how Kongzi employed men. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Gongchuo was by nature of few desires; the house elder of Zhao or Wei had no official duties, so he would have room to spare; the grandees of small states like Teng and Xue had many duties, so he could not do it. Variant: He Yan's text writes 藤 for 滕 and ends 大夫也.

sentences.t:
子路問成人。
子曰：「
若臧武仲之知，
公綽之不欲，
卞莊子之勇，
冉求之藝，
文之以禮樂，
亦可以為成人矣。」
