sentences.l:
Zilu asked about the whole man.
The Master said: “Like Zang Wuzhong's knowledge,
Gongchuo's freedom from desire,
Zhuangzi of Bian's courage,
Ran Qiu's skills —
pattern him with the rites and music,
and he too can count as a whole man.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked what makes a man whole. The Master said: “Take one who has Zang Wuzhong's understanding, Gongchuo's freedom from wants, the courage of Zhuangzi of Bian and Ran Qiu's many skills, and give it all form with the rites and music: such a man, too, may be called whole.”
sentences.n: 成人 'the made, complete man' — Zhu Xi: like saying 'the whole man' (全人). 若 'like' governs four phrases X之Y 'X's Y', and 文之以禮樂 'pattern him with the rites and music' is the condition laid on all four: 文 is a verb, 'to give pattern, form', and 樂 is yuè. 知 is read zhì, 'knowledge, wisdom' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), as 9.28. Zhu Xi: Wuzhong was a grandee of Lu named He 紇; Zhuangzi was grandee of the town of Bian in Lu (He Yan's Ma Rong: Zangsun He; Ma Rong: Gongchuo is Meng Gongchuo; Zhou Shenglie: grandee of Bian). Combine the strengths of these four, Zhu Xi says — knowledge enough to get to the bottom of principle, integrity enough to nourish the heart, courage enough to act with strength, skill enough to meet every case — and then measure it by the rites and bring it to harmony by music, so that virtue is formed within and pattern shows without: talent whole and virtue complete, all of a piece, with no trace of any one good to make a name by. But 亦 'too' shows this is not the highest: he speaks to what Zilu could reach; to speak of the highest, only the sage who fulfils the human way would do. Kong Anguo: add the rites and music to them, and the pattern is complete (文成也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 子路問成人曰, with no 子 before 曰, so the answer is not marked as the Master's; it writes 智 for 知 (the same word).

sentences.t:
曰：「
今之成人者何必然？
見利思義，
見危授命，
久要不忘平生之言，
亦可以為成人矣。」

morph.gloss: to grow, to be born, to arise

sentences.i: He went on: “But why must the whole man of our day be all that? If at the sight of gain he thinks first of what is right, if in the face of danger he will lay down his life, and if he does not forget a promise made long ago in the ordinary course of things — he too may be called whole.”
sentences.n: 何必然 'why necessarily so?'. 見 jiàn 'seeing'. 授命 'to hand over one's life' — Zhu Xi: not grudging one's life but taking it and giving it to another. 久要 'a long-standing 要': 要 yāo is a pledge, an agreement (Zhu Xi: 舊約也; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same), and 平生 is one's ordinary days (Zhu Xi: 平日也; Kong Anguo: 'when young', 猶少時). Who speaks? Zhu Xi: the added 曰 means that, having answered, the Master spoke again; one with the substance of wholeheartedness and good faith, though his talent, knowledge, rites and music fall short, may be the whole man of the next grade. He quotes Hu Yin: from 今之成人 on these are Zilu's words — he no longer had the courage to act at once on what he heard (11.21) but had the fixity of reciting a thing all his life (9.26); and Zhu Xi adds that he is not sure this is so (未詳是否). He quotes Master Cheng: clear knowledge, firm good faith and resolute action are the virtues common to all the world, and Kongzi's whole man does not go beyond these three: Wuzhong is knowledge, Gongchuo humaneness, Zhuangzi courage, Ran Qiu skill; one must unite these four men's powers and pattern them with the rites and music — yet great completion goes further still; and the whole man of today, who has good faith but does not reach the rites and music, is of the next grade again. Master Cheng again: Zang Wuzhong's knowledge was not upright, but patterned by the rites and music it would be upright through and through; and: who but a sage could bear the name 'whole man'? — as Mencius says, only the sage can fulfil his bodily form (踐形). He Yan's Ma Rong on 見利思義: he takes only when it is right, and does not grab.

sentences.t:
子問公叔文子於公明賈曰：「
信乎夫子不言、不笑、不取乎？」

words.reading: 公叔文子 gōng shū wén zǐ

morph.gloss: Gongshu Wenzi — a grandee of Wei
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Gongming Jia — a man of Wei
Jia, in the name Wangsun Jia
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master asked Gongming Jia about Gongshu Wenzi, saying:
“Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, does not take?”
sentences.i: The Master asked Gongming Jia about Gongshu Wenzi: “Is it true that your master never speaks, never laughs and never accepts anything?”
sentences.n: 信乎 'is it true?' put first, then the matter asked about, ending again in 乎 — 'true, that…?'. 夫子 'that master' here is Wenzi, Gongming Jia's master, not Confucius. Zhu Xi: Gongshu Wenzi was a grandee of Wei, Gongsun Zhi 公孫枝 (the print has 衛大失, for 衛大夫); Gongming is the surname and Jia the name, also a man of Wei. What kind of man Wenzi was cannot be known in detail, but he must have been clean and quiet, so in his day he was praised for these three things. He Yan's Kong Anguo names him Gongsun Ba (公孫㧞) and says 文 is his posthumous name.

sentences.t:
公明賈對曰：「
以告者過也。
夫子時然後言，人不厭其言；
樂然後笑，人不厭其笑；
義然後取，人不厭其取。」
子曰：「
其然？
豈其然乎？」

morph.gloss: Jia, in the name Wangsun Jia
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Gongming Jia replied: “Whoever told you that went too far. My master speaks only when the time is right, so no one is weary of his talk; he laughs only when something truly pleases him, so no one is weary of his laughter; he accepts a thing only when it is right to, so no one resents his taking.” The Master said: “Is that so? Can it really be so?”
sentences.n: 以告者 'those who reported (it)': 以 'by way of, thereby' + 告 'to tell', made a noun by 者. 過 'to overshoot'. Three lines of one shape: X然後Y 'X, and only then Y', followed by 人不厭其Y 'people do not tire of his Y'. 樂 is lè 'glad'. Zhu Xi: 厭 is to be sick of a thing because there is too much of it; when what a man does exactly fits what is fitting, people do not tire of it and do not even notice he does it — so the praise overshot and said that he did not speak, laugh or take. But this, Zhu Xi says, no one can do unless the rites and what is right fill him within and he has the timeliness of acting as the moment requires; Wenzi, worthy as he was, perhaps did not reach it; but the gentleman sides with men in doing good and does not like to name their faults outright, so he said 'Is that so? How could it be so?' — doubting it. 其然 'is it so?' with 其 marking a wondering question; 豈其然乎 'how could it be so?'. He Yan's Ma Rong: he admired his having gained the Way, but suspected he could not be wholly so. Variant: He Yan's text adds 也 after each of 人不厭其言, 其笑, 其取.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
臧武仲以防求為後於魯，
雖曰不要君，
吾不信也。」

morph.gloss: Zang (the Zangsun house of Lu, in 臧文仲)
Wu, posthumous name of Meng Wubo
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.i: The Master said: “Zang Wuzhong held on to Fang and from there asked Lu to appoint an heir to his house. He may say he was not putting pressure on his lord, but I do not believe it.”
sentences.n: 以防 'by means of Fang'; 求為後於魯 'sought to have (an heir) set up in Lu': 為後 wéi hòu is 'to set up an heir' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 為後，立後也). 要 yāo is 'to coerce' (Zhu Xi: 平聲; 有挾而求也, to make a demand while holding something over a man). Zhu Xi: Fang was a place, the town granted to Wuzhong. Wuzhong offended, fled to Zhu (邾), went from Zhu to Fang, and sent to ask that an heir be set up for his house, offering to leave the town — implying that if the request was refused he would hold the town in revolt: that is coercing the lord. He quotes Fan Zuyu: to coerce one's lord is to have no superior, a great crime; Wuzhong had received his town from his lord, and once he had offended and fled, setting up an heir lay with the lord, not his to decide; to hold the town while he asked came of loving cleverness and not loving learning. And Yang Shi: Wuzhong asked for an heir in humble words; outwardly it was not coercion, but in intent it was; the Master's words follow the Chunqiu's way of condemning the intention. Kong Anguo tells the story (the print dates it to Duke Xiang of Lu's thirty-third year): driven out by the slanders of the Meng house, Wuzhong fled to Zhu, went from Zhu to Fang, and sent a great tortoise with the message, 'I, He, dare not do harm; my wisdom was not enough. I do not presume to ask for myself; if only the ancestral sacrifices may be kept and the two meritorious forebears not abandoned, how should I dare not leave the town?' So Zang Wei (臧為) was set up as heir; He handed over Fang and fled to Qi.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
晉文公譎而不正，
齊桓公正而不譎。」

morph.gloss: Jin, the great state of the north (晉文公, 14.16)
to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)
Huan: Duke Huan of Song, from whom the Huan clan descends (Zhu Xi: 出於桓公故又稱桓氏)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Duke Wen of Jin was wily and not upright;
Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not wily.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Duke Wen of Jin was devious and not straight; Duke Huan of Qi was straight and not devious.”
sentences.n: A chiasmus: 譎而不正 / 正而不譎. 譎 jué (Zhu Xi: 古穴反) is 'crafty, deceitful' (Zhu Xi: 詭也; He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 詐也). Zhu Xi: Duke Wen of Jin was named Chong'er (重耳), Duke Huan of Qi Xiaobai (小白). Both were leaders of the lords' covenants who drove back the barbarians and honoured the Zhou royal house; and though both used force while borrowing the name of humaneness, and neither was upright at heart, Duke Huan, attacking Chu, relied on what was right and stated his case openly, not by devious ways — still better than the other; while Duke Wen attacked Wei to draw Chu out and won by secret plotting, which was crafty indeed. Their other doings were mostly of a piece with this, so the Master set them side by side to bring out what was hidden. Zheng Xuan: Wen's craft was summoning the Son of Heaven and making the lords attend him at court; Zhongni said a subject summoning his lord could not be a lesson, so the Chunqiu writes 'the Heavenly King hunted at Heyang'. Ma Rong: Huan, attacking Chu, invoked public right to reproach it for the thatch-grass tribute not sent in, and asked after King Zhao, who went south and never returned — upright, not crafty.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
桓公殺公子糾，
召忽死之，
管仲不死。」
曰：「
未仁乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Huan: Duke Huan of Song, from whom the Huan clan descends (Zhu Xi: 出於桓公故又稱桓氏)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Jiu, in the name Prince Jiu 公子糾 (14.17, 14.18)
suddenly, in a flash (忽焉在後 'then suddenly it is behind')
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.i: Zilu said: “When Duke Huan had Prince Jiu killed, Shao Hu died with his master, but Guan Zhong did not.” And he added: “Surely that falls short of humaneness?”
sentences.n: 糾 is the name Jiū (Zhu Xi spells it 居黝反, jiǔ; modern usage reads jiū); 召 is read shào (Zhu Xi: 音邵). 死之 'died for him', the verb 'to die' with an object, the one died for. The second 曰 is Zilu again, adding his verdict after a pause: 未仁乎 'not yet humane?', a question that expects agreement. Zhu Xi tells the story from the Chunqiu commentary: Duke Xiang of Qi was without the Way; Bao Shuya (鮑叔牙) took Prince Xiaobai and fled to Ju (莒); when Wuzhi (無知) murdered Duke Xiang, Guan Yiwu (Guan Zhong) and Shao Hu took Prince Jiu and fled to Lu. Lu tried to install Jiu and failed, and Xiaobai got in first — he is Duke Huan. He made Lu kill Jiu and asked for Guan and Shao to be handed over; Shao Hu died for his prince, Guan Zhong asked to be made a prisoner, and Bao Shuya spoke for him to Duke Huan, who made him his minister. Zilu suspected that Guan Zhong forgot his lord and served his enemy, a hardness of heart that wounds principle, and could not count as humane. He Yan's Kong Anguo tells the same story.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
桓公九合諸侯，
不以兵車，
管仲之力也。
如其仁！
如其仁！」

morph.gloss: Huan: Duke Huan of Song, from whom the Huan clan descends (Zhu Xi: 出於桓公故又稱桓氏)
the fused 之於 'it to, it at'
a lord, a feudal prince, ruler of a state (諸侯, 11.25)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Duke Huan nine times gathered the feudal lords,
not by war chariots:
it was Guan Zhong's strength.
Who matches his humaneness!
Who matches his humaneness!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “That Duke Huan could call the lords together time after time without resorting to war chariots was Guan Zhong's doing. Who can match his humaneness? Who can match it?”
sentences.n: 九合 'nine times gathered': Zhu Xi notes that the Chunqiu commentary writes 糾 for 九, which he glosses 督 'to marshal' (督也), the two being used for each other in old writing — so 'gathered and united'. The translation keeps the plain numeral, 'nine times', against Zhu Xi here (on his reading: 'Duke Huan gathered and united the feudal lords'); we print jiǔ. 合 hé 'to assemble'. 不以兵車 'not by war chariots', 車 chē — Zhu Xi: not relying on armed might. X之力也 'it was X's strength', that is, his doing. 如其仁 'who is like his humaneness?' — Zhu Xi: 誰如其仁者, and it is said twice to approve him deeply; He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it the same way, 'who is as humane as Guan Zhong?'. Zhu Xi: though Guan Zhong cannot be counted a humane man, his benefits reached the people, so he had the achievement of humaneness. Compare 3.22, where the Master finds his capacity small.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
管仲非仁者與？
桓公殺公子糾，
不能死，
又相之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “Guan Zhong was not a humane one, was he?
Duke Huan killed Prince Jiu;
he could not die,
and moreover he assisted him.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Surely Guan Zhong was not a humane man? When Duke Huan had Prince Jiu put to death, Guan Zhong could not die with his master — and then he went on to serve Duke Huan as his minister.”
sentences.n: Zigong raises the doubt Zilu raised in 14.17. 管仲 Guan Zhong (3.22) first served 公子糾 Prince Jiu of Qi; when Jiu's brother 桓公 Duke Huan (r. 685–643 BC) took the throne, Jiu was killed, Shao Hu, who had served Jiu with him, died with him, and Guan Zhong, recommended by Bao Shuya, became Huan's chief minister (the story is in Zhu Xi's note to 14.17). 糾 jiū (Zhu Xi at 14.17: 居黝反; modern jiū). 非仁者與 'not a humane one, was he?': 與 yú is a final question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲) that asks for agreement. 殺 shā 'to kill'. 不能死 'could not die' — did not die for his lord. 相 xiàng 'to assist', to serve as minister (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 之 'him' is Duke Huan. Zhu Xi: Zigong meant that not dying might still pass, but to go on and serve as Huan's minister was too much (子貢意不死猶可，相之則已甚矣).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
管仲相桓公，
霸諸侯，
一匡天下，
民到于今受其賜。
微管仲，
吾其被髮左衽矣。」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
the fused 之於 'it to, it at'
a lord, a feudal prince, ruler of a state (諸侯, 11.25)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Guan Zhong, assisting Duke Huan,
made him head of the feudal lords,
once and for all set right the world;
the people down to now receive his bounty.
Were it not for Guan Zhong,
we would surely let our hair hang loose and fold our robes on the left.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “As Duke Huan's minister, Guan Zhong made him leader of all the lords and set the whole world straight at a stroke; people are still enjoying the benefit today. Had there been no Guan Zhong, we should all have our hair hanging loose and our robes fastened on the left, like the barbarians.”
sentences.n: 相 xiàng 'to assist' (as unit 23). 霸 bà: Zhu Xi: 霸 is the same word as 伯 'eldest', and means 'to be head' (霸與伯同，長也) — with Guan Zhong's help Duke Huan became the first of the hegemons, the leaders of the lords. 匡 kuāng 'to set right' (Zhu Xi and Ma Rong: 匡，正也); 一 'once, at one stroke'. Zhu Xi: honouring the house of Zhou and driving back the Yi and Di tribes were both ways of setting the world right. Ma Rong (in He Yan): the Son of Heaven was weak, and Duke Huan led the lords in honouring the house of Zhou, setting the whole world right at once. 到于今 'reaching to now': 于 = 於. 賜 'what is bestowed, a bounty'. 微 'were it not for' (Zhu Xi and Ma Rong: 微，無也). 其 before the verb: 'surely, would'. 被 pī 'to let hang loose' (Zhu Xi: 皮寄反; modern pī); 髮 fà 'the hair of the head'; 衽 rèn 'the front flap of a robe' (Zhu Xi: 衣衿也; 而審反), and 左衽 is closing it on the left side. Zhu Xi: loose hair and robes closed on the left are the customs of the Yi and Di. He Yan's own comment: 'receive his bounty' means the boon of not wearing loose hair and left-closed robes; Ma Rong: without Guan Zhong, lords would not be lords nor ministers ministers, and all would have become Yi and Di. The Master's answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
豈若匹夫匹婦之為諒也，
自經於溝瀆而莫之知也？
sentences.l:
How would he be like common men and common women keeping their petty good faith,
hanging themselves in a ditch or a drain and no one knowing of it?
sentences.i: Would you have had him be like some common man or woman who, to keep a small promise, strangles himself in a ditch, and nobody ever hears of it?
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted. 豈若…也 'how would he be like…?', a rhetorical question. 匹夫匹婦 'a single man, a single woman': ordinary people of no standing (匹夫 'a lone commoner' at 9.25). 之 makes 'common men and women practising petty good faith' one phrase. 諒 liàng: Zhu Xi: 諒，小信也 'small good faith', keeping one's word in a small matter. 經 jīng is here 'to hang oneself' (Zhu Xi: 經，縊也). 溝 'a ditch', 瀆 dú 'a drain, a channel'. 莫之知 'no one knows of them': the pronoun 之 stands before the verb after 莫. Zhu Xi: 莫之知 means others do not know; the History of the Later Han, quoting this, has 人 before 莫. He quotes Master Cheng: Duke Huan was the elder brother and Jiu the younger; Guan Zhong, privately helping the man he served to contend for the state, was not doing right; Huan went too far in killing Jiu, yet Jiu's death was his due. Having plotted with him, Guan Zhong might have died with him; knowing that helping him contend was not right, he might also save himself to seek later achievement — so the sage did not blame him for not dying and praised what he achieved. Had Huan been the younger and Jiu the elder, Huan would have been an enemy Guan Zhong could not live under the same sky with, and for the sage to weigh his later achievement and approve his serving Huan would have done great harm to what is right and opened the way to faithless turncoats for ten thousand ages — like Wang Gui and Wei Zheng of the Tang, who did not die with Jiancheng and went over to Taizong: whatever they later achieved, how could it redeem that? Zhu Xi adds his own view (愚謂): Guan Zhong had achievement and no guilt, so the sage praised only his achievement; Wang and Wei had guilt first and achievement after, and one may rightly refuse to let the one cover the other. Wang Su (in He Yan): 經 is dying by hanging, in a ditch; the comment goes on that between Guan Zhong and Shao Hu and Prince Jiu the bond of lord and minister was not yet fully set, so dying for him deserved no deep praise and not dying no great blame — hence the Master praised only Guan Zhong's achievement, and did not say Shao Hu was wrong to die.

sentences.t:
公叔文子之臣大夫僎，
與文子同升諸公。

words.reading: 公叔文子 gōng shū wén zǐ

sentences.l:
Gongshu Wenzi's retainer, the grandee Zhuan,
rose together with Wenzi to the duke's court.
sentences.i: Zhuan, who had been a retainer in Gongshu Wenzi's household, became a grandee and went up to the duke's court side by side with Wenzi himself.
sentences.n: 公叔文子 Gongshu Wenzi is the grandee of Wei of 14.14. 臣 is here a household retainer (Zhu Xi: 臣，家臣). 僎 zhuàn is the retainer's personal name (Zhu Xi: 士免反). 升 'to go up, rise'. 諸 is the fused 之於 'him to', or simply 'to'; 公 is the duke's court (Zhu Xi: 公，公朝). Zhu Xi: it means Wenzi recommended him, so that he went forward with Wenzi himself to be a minister at the ducal court. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): the grandee Zhuan had been Wenzi's household retainer; Wenzi recommended him and made him a grandee alongside himself, so that they rose together at the duke's court.

sentences.t:
子聞之，曰：「
可以為文矣。」
sentences.l: The Master heard of it and said: “He can well be named Wen, ‘cultured’.”
sentences.i: When the Master heard of it he said: “He has earned his name of Wen, ‘cultured’.”
sentences.n: 文 Wen 'cultured' was Gongshu Wenzi's posthumous title, as it was Kong Wenzi's (5.14); 可以為文 'can thereby count as Wen' — this act alone shows the title deserved. Zhu Xi: 文 means following principle so that it forms a pattern (順理而成章); and the rules for posthumous titles also have 'bestowing rank and office on the people is called Wen' (錫民爵位曰文). He quotes Mr Hong (洪氏): to take a household retainer, a lowly man, and draw him up to stand beside oneself shows three good things — knowing men, forgetting oneself, and serving one's lord. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): conduct like this deserves the posthumous title Wen.

sentences.t:
子言衛靈公之無道也，
康子曰：「
夫如是，
奚而不喪？」

morph.gloss: Kang, posthumous name of Ji Kangzi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master spoke of Duke Ling of Wei's lacking the Way.
Kangzi said: “Now, being like this,
how is it he does not lose his place?”
sentences.i: The Master was speaking of how Duke Ling of Wei paid no heed to the Way. Kangzi said: “If he is like that, how is it he has not lost his throne?”
sentences.n: 衛靈公 Duke Ling of Wei (r. 534–493 BC), in whose state the Master spent years of his travels; Nanzi of 6.26 was his wife. 無道 'without the Way', of a ruler: lawless, misgoverning. 之 makes 'Duke Ling's being without the Way' one phrase, the object of 言 'spoke of'. 康子 Kangzi is Ji Kangzi, head of the Ji house of Lu (10.11). 夫 fú opens the sentence: 'now' (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 奚而 'how is it that'. 喪 sàng 'to lose' (Zhu Xi: 去聲) — Zhu Xi: 喪 is losing his place (失位). Variant: He Yan's text reads 子曰衛霊公之無道也 'The Master said: “Duke Ling of Wei is without the Way”' — 曰 'said' for 言 'spoke of'.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
仲叔圉治賓客，
祝鮀治宗廟，
王孫賈治軍旅。
夫如是，
奚其喪？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
an invocator, the temple officer who speaks the prayers (Zhu Xi: 祝，宗廟之官)
Tuo: the invocator Tuo of Wei (Zhu Xi: 鮀徒何反)
to take as chief, to look up to as head (Zhu Xi: 主)
Sun, 'grandson', the clan name's last part (孟孫, 季孫, 仲孫)
Jia, in the name Wangsun Jia

sentences.l:
Kongzi said: “Zhongshu Yu manages guests and visitors,
the invocator Tuo manages the ancestral temple,
Wangsun Jia manages the army and troops.
Now, being like this,
how would he lose it?”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “He has Zhongshu Yu to look after his guests and envoys, the invocator Tuo to take charge of the ancestral temple, and Wangsun Jia to command his armies. With men like that, why should he lose his throne?”
sentences.n: 仲叔圉 Zhongshu Yu is Kong Wenzi of 5.14 (Zhu Xi: 仲叔圉即孔文子也); 祝鮀 is the invocator Tuo of 6.14, 王孫賈 Wangsun Jia of 3.13. 治 'to manage, have charge of'. 賓客 'guests and visitors' — envoys from other states. 宗廟 'the ancestral temple' and its sacrifices. 軍 and 旅 are both bodies of troops: together, 'the army'. 奚其喪 'how would he lose it?', 其 adding doubt. Zhu Xi: all three were ministers of Wei; not necessarily worthy men, but their talents were of use, and Duke Ling used them, each in the post that fitted his talent. He quotes Yin Tun: Duke Ling of Wei's lack of the Way should have lost him his state, yet by using these three he could still keep it — how much more a ruler who has the Way and can use the worthy and able of the whole world! As the Ode says: 'Nothing is stronger than having the men; the four quarters take him for their pattern' (無競維人，四方其訓之). Kong Anguo (in He Yan): though the lord lacks the Way, those he employs are each fit for their tasks — why should he be ruined?

sentences.t:
子曰：「
其言之不怍，
則為之也難。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If his speaking of it is without shame,
then doing it is hard.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man who can talk big without a blush will find his words hard to live up to.”
sentences.n: 其言之不怍 'his speaking of it not being abashed' is the condition, 則 'then' the result. 怍 zuò 'to be ashamed, abashed'. 為之也難: 也 sets off 為之 'doing it' as the topic — 'as for doing it, hard'; 為 wéi, 難 nán. Zhu Xi: one who talks big without shame has no firm resolve to do it and does not weigh whether he can; when he comes to make his words good, will it not be hard? Ma Rong (in He Yan) reads it otherwise: 怍 is 'shame' (慙); one who has the reality within speaks of it without shame; to build up that reality is what is hard. (He Yan's print gives his gloss as 作，慙也, a slip for 怍.) Variant: He Yan's text reads 則其為之難也 'then his doing it is hard'.

sentences.t: 陳成子弑簡公。
sentences.l: Chen Chengzi assassinated Duke Jian.
sentences.i: Chen Chengzi murdered his lord, Duke Jian of Qi.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Chengzi was a grandee of Qi, personal name Heng 恒; Duke Jian was the ruler of Qi, personal name Ren 壬; the event is recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals under the fourteenth year of Duke Ai (481 BC). 弑 shì is the word for a subject killing his lord (5.18). Variant: He Yan's text has 殺 'killed' for 弑, here and in the next unit — the plain word, not the one that names the crime.

sentences.t:
孔子沐浴而朝，
告於哀公曰：「陳恒弑其君，
請討之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Kongzi washed and bathed and went to court. He told Duke Ai: “Chen Heng has murdered his lord. I ask you to bring him to justice.”
sentences.n: 沐 mù is washing the hair, 浴 washing the body. 朝 cháo 'to go to court' (Zhu Xi: 音潮). 哀公 Duke Ai of Lu (2.19). Kongzi calls the murderer by his personal name, Heng (恒 héng). 請 'I ask (leave to)'; 討 tǎo 'to punish, to bring to account'. Zhu Xi: at this time Kongzi had retired from office and was living in Lu; he bathed and fasted (沐浴齊戒) before telling his lord, treating the matter as weighty and not daring to take it lightly. A subject's murder of his lord is the greatest overturning of the human bonds, what Heaven's principle cannot bear; any man may put the murderer to death, how much more a neighbouring state. So though the Master had already retired for age, he still asked Duke Ai to punish him. Ma Rong (in He Yan): Chen Chengzi is Chen Heng, grandee of Qi; about to report to the lord, Kongzi first fasted, and fasting requires bathing. Variant: He Yan's text reads 陳桓殺其君 — 殺 for 弑, and 桓 for 恒, perhaps a copying slip (Ma Rong's comment there also writes 陳桓).

sentences.t:
公曰：「
告夫三子。」
sentences.l: The Duke said: “Tell those three masters.”
sentences.i: The Duke said: “Tell the three of them.”
sentences.n: 夫 fú is here 'those' (Zhu Xi: the 夫 of both 告夫 is read 扶). 三子 'the three masters': Zhu Xi: the three houses — the Three Families (三家) of 3.2, the Mengsun, Shusun and Jisun; at this time government lay with them and Duke Ai could not act on his own, so he had Kongzi tell them. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): it means the three ministers (三卿). Variant: He Yan's text reads 告夫二三子 'tell those gentlemen', with the 二三子 'my friends' by which the Master addresses his disciples at 7.23, here and in the next two units.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
以吾従大夫之後，
不敢不告也。
君曰：『告夫三子』者！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said: “Because I follow at the rear of the grandees,
I dare not fail to report.
And my lord says, ‘Tell those three masters’!”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Because I still have a place, at the back, among the grandees, I dared not leave it unreported. And my lord tells me, ‘Tell the three of them’!”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Kongzi went out and said this to himself. His meaning: a murderer of his lord is one the law must punish; a grandee takes counsel for the state, and what is right requires him to report; yet the lord cannot himself give the order to the three, and sends me to tell them! 以吾従大夫之後 'because I follow at the rear of the grandees' — Kongzi's modest way of saying he still held a grandee's rank, as in 11.7; 以 'because'; 従 cóng is the edition's form of 從. 不敢不告 'dare not not report'. 者 closes the clause that quotes the Duke's order — 'that he should say…!' — and Zhu Xi reads the line as a protest. Ma Rong (in He Yan): by the rites I ought to report to the lord, not to the three; but since the lord sends me, I go on to them.

sentences.t:
之三子告，不可。
孔子曰：「
以吾従大夫之後，
不敢不告也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He went to the three masters and reported; they would not agree.
Kongzi said: “Because I follow at the rear of the grandees,
I dare not fail to report.”
sentences.i: He went and told the three; they refused. Kongzi said: “Because I still have a place, at the back, among the grandees, I dared not leave it unreported.”
sentences.n: 之 is here the verb 'to go to'. 不可 'not acceptable': they refused. Zhu Xi: he went to report at his lord's command; but the three were the over-mighty ministers of Lu, long minded to do without a lord, and in fact leaned on the Chen house for power and standing, so they blocked his plan; and the Master again answered them with these words — a deep warning to them. He quotes Master Cheng: the Zuo Commentary records Kongzi as saying, 'Chen Heng has killed his lord, and half the people are not with him; add the multitude of Lu to half of Qi and we can win' — these are not Kongzi's words; if he had said this, he would be relying on force, not on what is right. Kongzi's intent would have been to name the crime rightly, report it up to the Son of Heaven and down to the leading lord of the region, and lead the allied states to punish him; how to defeat Qi was a lesser matter for him — would he reckon up the numbers of Lu? The world's disorder was then at its height; by this it could have been set right, and the house of Zhou risen again. That the lord and ministers of Lu would not follow him is more than can be regretted. And Hu Yin: by the law of the Spring and Autumn Annals anyone may punish a murderer of his lord; in this act Zhongni could even have struck first and reported afterwards (先𤼵後聞). Ma Rong (in He Yan): Kongzi went to the three at the lord's command; they refused, so he answered with these words and let it rest. Variant: He Yan's text reads 之二三子告, and the last 不敢不告 lacks 也.

sentences.t:
子路問事君。
子曰：「
勿欺也，
而犯之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu asked about serving a lord.
The Master said: “Do not deceive him,
and then stand up to him.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked how to serve a lord. The Master said: “Never deceive him; then, when you must, oppose him to his face.”
sentences.n: 勿 'do not'. 犯 'to offend against' — Zhu Xi: 犯 means to brave the lord's displeasure, remonstrating and contending with him (犯謂犯顔諫爭). He quotes Fan Zuyu: offending was not what Zilu found hard; not deceiving was what was hard for him, so the Master taught him first not to deceive and then to offend. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): in the way of serving a lord, what is right forbids deceiving him; one should be able to brave his displeasure, remonstrating and contending (犯顔色諫争).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子上達，
小人下達。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman gets through upward;
the small man gets through downward.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman makes his way up, the small man makes his way down.”
sentences.n: 上 'upward' and 下 'downward' are used as adverbs before 達 'to get through, to reach'. Zhu Xi: the gentleman follows Heaven's principle, so day by day he advances toward the high and bright; the small man follows human desire, so day by day he goes further into the foul and low (日究乎汙下). He Yan's own comment reads it otherwise: the root is above, the branch tips below (本為上，未為下, where the print's 未 is evidently a slip for 末 'branch tip') — the gentleman reaches the root of things, the small man only the branches.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
古之學者為己，
今之學者為人。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The learners of old were for themselves;
the learners of today are for others.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “In the old days men studied to make something of themselves; nowadays they study to be noticed by others.”
sentences.n: 古之學者 'those of old who learned', 今之學者 'those of today who learn'. 為 wèi 'for, for the sake of' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: 'for oneself' is wanting to get it in oneself; 'for others' is wanting to be known by others. And Master Cheng again: those of old who learned for themselves ended by bringing others to completion (成物); those of today who learn for others end by losing themselves. Zhu Xi adds: sages and worthies have said much about where learners go right or wrong in how they set their minds, but nothing as pointed and essential as this; distinguish it clearly here and examine oneself by it daily, and one will hardly be in the dark about what to follow. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): learning for oneself is treading it and doing it; learning for others is merely being able to talk of it. Variant: He Yan's text ends 今之學者為人也, with a final particle.

sentences.t: 蘧伯玉使人於孔子。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Qu Boyu sent a man to Kongzi.
sentences.i: Qu Boyu sent a messenger to Kongzi.
sentences.n: 蘧伯玉 Qu Boyu was a grandee of Wei, personal name Yuan 瑗 (Zhu Xi; Kong Anguo in He Yan); 伯玉 is his courtesy name. Zhu Xi: when Kongzi lived in Wei he once lodged at his house; afterwards he went back to Lu, and so Boyu sent someone to him. 使 'to send on a mission': Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, here and below — the old reading shì, 'envoy, to go or send as envoy'; modern Mandarin reads shǐ, which we give.

sentences.t:
孔子與之坐而問焉，曰：「
夫子何為？」
對曰：「
夫子欲寡其過而未能也。」
使者出。
子曰：「
使乎！使乎！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi sat with him and asked him, saying: “What does your master do?”
He answered, saying: “My master wants to make his faults few, but is not yet able.”
The one who was sent went out.
The Master said: “A messenger, that! A messenger, that!”
sentences.i: Kongzi gave him a seat and asked: “What is your master doing these days?” He answered: “My master is trying to have fewer faults, and has not yet managed it.” When the messenger had gone, the Master said: “There goes a true messenger — a true messenger!”
sentences.n: 與之坐 'sat with him' — Zhu Xi: giving him a seat honoured his master, and the honour reached his messenger. 焉 'of him'. 夫子 'that master' here means Boyu (Zhu Xi: 夫子指伯玉也), not the Master. 何為 'does what?' — the question word stands before the verb; 為 wéi. 寡其過 'to make his faults few'. 使者 'the one sent', the messenger; 使乎 'a messenger, that!' — 乎 exclaims. Zhu Xi: in saying only that Boyu wanted fewer faults and still could not manage it, the messenger let one see his master's constant sense of falling short as he examined himself and overcame himself; the humbler the messenger's words, the more plainly his master's worth shone. He knew the gentleman's heart deeply and was good with words, so the Master said 'a messenger!' twice, to praise him the more. Zhu Xi adds that Zhuang Zhou says Boyu, at fifty, knew the wrongs of his forty-nine years, and at sixty had changed sixty times: his work of advancing in virtue did not flag in old age, so his conduct was solid and its light shone forth, and not only his messenger knew it — the Master trusted it too. He Yan's own comment: his master wanted to make his faults few, but could not yet be without faults. Chen Qun (in He Yan): saying 'a messenger!' twice is praise — the mission had found the right man. Variant: He Yan's text reads 孔子與人坐 'Kongzi sat with the man', perhaps a slip for 之.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不在其位，
不謀其政。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not being in the post,
one does not lay plans for its government.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If the office is not yours, leave the planning of its business alone.”
sentences.n: The saying of 8.14, word for word, and given the same English; Zhu Xi marks it 重出 'it comes out again'. Two clauses of four characters; the first, with no marker, is the condition of the second, and the two 其 point to the same office. In the Ruan witness as transcribed, this chapter and the next stand under one number.

sentences.t:
曽子曰：「
君子思不出其位。」

morph.gloss: Zeng (a surname; the edition's form of 曾)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Master Zeng said: “The gentleman in his thoughts does not go out of his post.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “A gentleman keeps his thinking within the bounds of his own post.”
sentences.n: 曽子 Master Zeng is the disciple Zeng Shen (1.4); 曽 is the edition's form of 曾 here. 思 'his thinking' is the subject; 出 'to go out of'. Zhu Xi: this is the Image text (象辭) of the hexagram 艮 'Keeping Still' in the Changes; Master Zeng had perhaps quoted it, and the compiler, prompted by the saying of the chapter before, set it down after it as of a kind. He quotes Fan Zuyu: when each thing rests in its own place, the order of the world is achieved; so the gentleman's thoughts do not go beyond his post, and lord and minister, high and low, great and small, all fulfil their offices. He Yan gives no comment on 14.27 or 14.28.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子恥其言，
而過其行。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is ashamed to go far in his words,
and goes beyond in his deeds.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman is shy of saying too much, and eager to do more than enough.”
sentences.n: Two halves of one shape, joined by 而 'and'. Zhu Xi: 恥 'to be ashamed' here means not daring to go the full length (不敢盡之意); 過 'to go beyond' means wanting to have more than enough (欲有餘之辭) — sparing in word, overflowing in deed (compare 4.22 and 4.24). 行 is 'conduct, deeds': Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, the old reading xìng for the noun; modern Mandarin reads xíng. Variant: He Yan's text reads 君子恥其言之過其行也 'the gentleman is ashamed that his words go beyond his deeds': with 之 for 而, 'his words going beyond his deeds' becomes one phrase, the object of 恥.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子道者三，
我無能焉：
仁者不憂，
知者不惑，
勇者不懼。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “There are three things in the gentleman's way, and I have managed none of them: the humane man has no cares, the man who knows is never at a loss, and the brave man has nothing he dreads.”
sentences.n: 道者三 'as for the ways, (they are) three': 者 marks the topic; 道 dào. 我無能焉 'I have no ability in them' — 焉 'in them'. The three lines are those of 9.28, with humaneness put first, and keep its English. 知 is zhì 'wise' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi: he blames himself to spur others on (自責以勉人也). He Yan gives no comment here.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
夫子自道也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zigong said: “The Master speaks of himself.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “The Master is describing himself.”
sentences.n: 道 dào is here the verb 'to say, to speak of' (Zhu Xi: 道，言也); 自 'oneself', drawn before the verb as its object. Zhu Xi: 'speaking of himself' is as if to say 'these are words of modesty' (自道猶云謙辭) — he has the three himself. He quotes Yin Tun: in completed virtue humaneness comes first; in advancing in learning, wisdom comes first — that is why the order of the Master's words differs (here and 9.28).

sentences.t:
子貢方人。
子曰：「
賜也賢乎哉？
夫我則不暇。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong compared people.
The Master said: “Ci — is he so worthy, then?
Now I, for my part, have no leisure for it.”
sentences.i: Zigong was given to weighing one man against another. The Master said: “So Ci is a worthy man, is he? I myself have no leisure to spare for it.”
sentences.n: 方 'to compare' (Zhu Xi: 方，比也; Kong Anguo in He Yan: 比方人也, measuring people against one another). 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name (1.15). 乎哉 ends a question of doubt (Zhu Xi: 疑辭). 夫 fú opens the sentence (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 暇 xiá 'leisure, spare time'. Zhu Xi: comparing people and weighing their strong and weak points is also a way of searching out principle; but give oneself wholly to it and the mind runs off outward, and the work of governing oneself grows slack. So the Master praised him in words of doubt, and then belittled himself, to check him the more. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: when the sage reproves a man, his words are not pressing, yet the point goes home, like this. Kong Anguo (in He Yan): he had no leisure for comparing people. Variant: He Yan's text reads 賜也賢乎我 'Ci, is he worthier than I?', probably a slip for 哉.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不患人之不己知，
患其不能也。」

morph.gloss: (makes 'others do not know me' into a noun phrase)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Be not troubled by others' not knowing oneself;
be troubled by one's own lack of ability.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Be troubled not that others do not know you, but that you are not capable.”
sentences.n: The first line is 1.16's and keeps its English: 之 makes 人之不己知 one noun phrase, and after the negative the pronoun object 己 stands before the verb. 其不能 'one's not being able' — 其 points back to oneself. Zhu Xi: where chapters share a point and the wording does not differ, it is one saying recorded twice; where the wording differs a little, it was said on several occasions and set down each time. This chapter appears four times (1.16, 4.14, here, and once more in Book 15), each time worded differently — so the sage said it often, and one can see how he pressed it home. Wang Su (in He Yan): only be troubled at one's own lack of ability. Variant: He Yan's text reads 患己無能也 'be troubled at having no ability oneself' (its print writes 巳 for 己).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不逆詐，
不億不信，
抑亦先覺者，
是賢乎！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not going out to meet deceit,
not guessing at lack of good faith,
yet still the one who perceives it beforehand —
this is the worthy one!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Not to go looking for deceit, nor to imagine in advance that others mistrust you, and yet to be the first to see it when it is there — that is true worth.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 逆 nì is going out to meet a thing before it has come; 億 is guessing at it before one has seen it; 詐 is others deceiving one, and 不信 others mistrusting one (詐謂人欺己，不信謂人疑己). 抑 marks the turn of the sentence (抑，反語辭): though one neither anticipates nor guesses, one perceives beforehand, quite naturally, what is true and false in men's feelings — that is worth. 覺 jué 'to perceive, to become aware'. He quotes Yang Shi: the gentleman is wholly sincere, and that is all; but there is no sincerity that is not also clear-sighted, so though he does not anticipate deceit or guess at mistrust, he always perceives first. Were one to neither anticipate nor guess and end by being fooled by small men, that too would not be worth looking at. Kong Anguo (in He Yan) takes the last line as a doubting question: one who perceives men's feelings beforehand — can that make him worthy? At times he ends by resenting others instead. Variant: He Yan's text writes 憶 for 億 (the same word 'to guess', with the heart radical).

sentences.t:
微生畝謂孔子曰：「
丘，何為是栖栖者與？
無乃為佞乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Weisheng Mu said to Kongzi, saying: “Qiu, why are you this clinging, restless one?
Is it not rather that you practise glibness?”
sentences.i: Weisheng Mu said to Kongzi: “Qiu, what keeps you hanging on everywhere, never at rest? Is it not that you make a trade of a clever tongue?”
sentences.n: 微生畝 Weisheng Mu: Zhu Xi says 微生 is the surname (as Weisheng Gao, 5.23) and 畝 the personal name; he calls the Master by his personal name, 丘 Qiu, and his words are very haughty, so he was probably a recluse of age and virtue (葢有齒徳而隠者). Bao Xian in He Yan gives only surname and name. 何為 'for what, why': 為 is wèi. 是栖栖者 'this restless one': 是 'this, such', 者 makes 栖栖 a person. 栖栖 xī xī (栖 = 棲 'to perch') Zhu Xi glosses 依依 'clinging, hanging on'. 無乃…乎 'is it not rather…?'. 與 is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). 為佞 'to practise glibness' (為 wéi): Zhu Xi, that he makes a business of a ready tongue to please people (務為口給以悦人).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
非敢為佞也，
疾固也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said: “It is not that I dare practise glibness;
I hate obstinacy.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “I would not presume to be a smooth talker. It is stubbornness I cannot abide.”
sentences.n: 非…也 'it is not that…', answered by a second 也 clause giving the real reason. 疾 jí is 'to hate' here (Zhu Xi: 疾，惡也), not 'illness'. 固 'obstinacy': Zhu Xi, holding to one thing and not getting through (執一而不通). He reads the reply as a warning to Mu himself: the sage, toward one honoured for age, is respectful in manner and straight in speech, and his warning to him is a deep one (聖人之於達尊禮恭而言直如此其警之亦深矣). Bao Xian in He Yan takes the obstinacy to be the world's: 'I chafe at the age's narrow obstinacy, and wish to put the Way in practice to change people' (疾丗固陋欲行道以化人也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 孔子對曰 'Kongzi answered', the word for replying to an elder or superior.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
驥不稱其力，
稱其徳也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A thoroughbred is not praised for its strength;
it is praised for its virtue.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What people praise in a fine horse is not its strength but its virtue — its good training and temper.”
sentences.n: 驥 jì is the name for a fine horse (Zhu Xi: 善馬之名). 稱 chēng 'to praise, to speak of'. A horse's 徳 'virtue' (徳 is the edition's form of 德) is, Zhu Xi says, its being well trained and good-tempered (調良); Zheng Xuan in He Yan says the same (德者謂調良之德也). Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: though a thoroughbred has strength, what it is praised for is its virtue; if a man has talent and no virtue, what is there in him worth esteeming? (人有才而無徳則亦奚足尚哉).

sentences.t:
或曰：「
以徳報怨，何如？」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.l: Someone said: “Repaying resentment with virtue — how is it?”
sentences.i: Someone said: “What do you say to answering a grudge with kindness?”
sentences.n: 以徳報怨 'with virtue to repay resentment': 以 'by means of' comes first, then the verb 報 bào 'to repay, to answer' and its object 怨 'resentment, a grudge' — the wrong someone has done one. Zhu Xi: this was a saying people quoted, now found in the book of Laozi (或人所稱今見老子書; Daodejing 63 has 報怨以德); here 徳 means a kindness done, a favour (徳謂恩惠也), and the i says 'kindness' for it. 何如 'how is it?' (1.15).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
何以報徳？」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Then with what does one repay virtue?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Then what would you answer kindness with?”
sentences.n: 何以 'with what': the question word 何 stands before 以, as an interrogative object of a preposition does. Zhu Xi: if one has already repaid with kindness those one resents, what is left to repay those who have done one kindness? The Master's answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
以直報怨，
以徳報徳。
sentences.l:
With straightness repay resentment;
with virtue repay virtue.
sentences.i: Answer a grudge with fair and straight dealing; a kindness done you, answer in kind.
sentences.n: Two lines of one shape, 以 X 報 Y. 直 'straight' is Zhu Xi's key word: toward the one he resents, a man's love and dislike, his taking and refusing, are all ruled by perfect fairness with nothing private in it — that is 'straightness' (愛憎取舍一以至公而無私所謂直也); toward one who has done him kindness he must repay kindness and never forget it. The questioner's saying, he goes on, may be called generous, but seen beside the sage's it comes from a private intention, and both repayments lose their balance; only the Master's way gives each its due — and since resentment is not avenged while every kindness is repaid, it too is generous. The words are plain and brief, but their meaning turns and returns, like the workings of nature, simple and easy to know yet endlessly subtle; learners should savour it closely.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
莫我知也夫！」
sentences.l: The Master said: “No one knows me — ah!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Ah — not one person knows me for what I am.”
sentences.n: 莫我知 is 莫知我 'no one knows me', with the pronoun object 我 drawn before the verb after the negative 莫 (as 13.15 莫予違). 也夫 a final sigh; 夫 is fú (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). Zhu Xi: the Master sighs to himself, so as to draw a question from Zigong (夫子自歎以發子貢之問也).

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
何為其莫知子也？」
子曰：「
不怨天，不尤人；
下學而上達。
知我者，其天乎！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “Why is it that no one knows you?”
The Master said: “I do not resent Heaven, do not blame others;
I learn below and get through above.
The one who knows me — surely it is Heaven!”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “How can it be that no one understands you?” The Master said: “I bear Heaven no grudge and lay no blame on men. I learn from the things close at hand and work my way through to what is high. If anyone understands me, it must be Heaven.”
sentences.n: 何為其…也 'why is it that…?' (為 wèi); 子 is 'you', addressed to the Master. 尤 'to blame'. 下學而上達: 下 and 上 are 'below' and 'above' used as adverbs — learning in the low, everyday things, getting through to the high ones. Zhu Xi: not finding favour with Heaven, he does not resent Heaven; not fitting with men, he does not blame men; he only knows to learn below and so of itself get through above. This is only his speaking of turning back on himself and cultivating himself step by step, nothing very different from others that would make him known; yet savoured deeply, it holds a mystery men cannot reach and Heaven alone knows. In the Kong school only Zigong's wisdom came near this, so the Master spoke to bring it out — a pity, Zhu Xi adds, that Zigong still did not quite get there. He quotes Master Cheng: 'not resenting Heaven, not blaming others — that is how it ought to be by principle'; 'in learning below and getting through above, the meaning lies beyond the words'; 'learners must hold to the words 下學上達; they are the key to learning.' The comment closes: learning the affairs of men below is itself getting through to the principle of Heaven above, but practise without examining it and one will not get through. In He Yan: its own comment says Zigong, puzzled at the Master's words, asked; Ma Rong — Kongzi, not used by his age, did not resent Heaven, and though men did not know him did not blame them; Kong Anguo — 下學 is learning the affairs of men, 上達 knowing the decree of Heaven above (上知天命); and He Yan's own comment: the sage matches Heaven and Earth in virtue, so he says only Heaven knows him.

sentences.t:
公伯寮愬子路於季孫。
子服景伯以告曰：「
夫子固有惑志於公伯寮；
吾力猶能肆諸市朝。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
Sun, 'grandson', the clan name's last part (孟孫, 季孫, 仲孫)

words.reading: 子服景伯 zǐ fú jǐng bó

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Liao, in the name 公伯寮 (14.38)

sentences.i: Gongbo Liao spoke against Zilu to the head of the Ji house. Zifu Jingbo came and told Kongzi of it: “His lordship has certainly let Gongbo Liao lead him astray. But I still have power enough to have the man put to death and his body shown in the market-place or at court.”
sentences.n: 公伯寮 Gongbo Liao was a man of Lu (Zhu Xi: 魯人); Ma Rong in He Yan makes him a disciple. 愬 sù here is to bring a complaint against someone, to slander (Ma Rong: 愬，譖也). 季孫 Jisun is the head of that house, the Ji clan by its full name (季氏, 3.1). 子服景伯 Zifu Jingbo: Zhu Xi — 子服 his house, 景 his posthumous name, 伯 his courtesy name, the Lu grandee Zifu He 子服何 (Ma Rong: 子服何忌). 以告 'reported it' — to Kongzi (Ma Rong). 夫子 here is not the Master but Jisun, 'that lord' (Zhu Xi: 夫子指季孫), who has doubts because of Liao's words. 肆 sì is to lay out a corpse for show (Zhu Xi: 陳尸也): Jingbo means he would have Liao put to death. 諸 = 之於 'him in'. 朝 is cháo 'the court' (Zhu Xi: 朝音潮). Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 'my power can make Jisun see that Zilu is blameless, and have Liao executed and laid out'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 惑志於公伯寮也, adding 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道之將行也與，命也；
道之將廢也與，命也。
公伯寮其如命何？」

morph.gloss: Liao, in the name 公伯寮 (14.38)

sentences.i: The Master said: “If the Way is to prevail, that is as it is decreed; if the Way is to be cast aside, that too is as it is decreed. What can Gongbo Liao do against that?”
sentences.n: 道之將行 'the Way's being about to prevail': 之 turns the clause into a topic; 將 jiāng 'about to'; 行 xíng 'to go forward, to prevail'; 廢 'to be cast aside'. 也與 closes each topic with a questioning lift — 與 is yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲) — and 命也 is the answer. 命 'what is decreed', the decree (12.5). 其如…何 'what could he do about…?' (as 7.22, 9.5). Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: even if Liao's slander had succeeded, that too would have been decree; in truth Liao could do nothing. And adds in his own voice (愚謂): the Master said this to enlighten Jingbo, settle Zilu and warn Liao; where gain and harm are concerned, the sage does not need to wait for the decree to decide before he is at ease.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
賢者辟世。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “The worthy avoid the age.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The worthiest of men withdraw from their age itself.”
sentences.n: 辟 is read bì, the word 'to avoid', later written 避 (Zhu Xi: 辟去聲, and so below); He Yan's text writes 避 throughout this chapter. 賢者 'the worthy'. Zhu Xi: when the world is without the Way they withdraw into hiding, like Boyi (5.22) and the Grand Duke (太公). Kong Anguo in He Yan: no ruler of the age can make them his ministers. The Master's saying runs on past Zhu Xi's comments; the next three units are left unquoted.

sentences.t: 其次辟地。
sentences.l: The next avoid a place.
sentences.i: Those next to them withdraw from a particular place.
sentences.n: 其次 'the next (after them)', the next grade (13.20). Zhu Xi: they leave a disordered state for a well-ruled one (去亂國適治邦) — Ma Rong in He Yan says the same.

sentences.t: 其次辟色。
sentences.l: The next avoid a look.
sentences.i: Those next, from a look on a ruler's face.
sentences.n: 色 'the face, the look'. Zhu Xi: when the courtesy of the ruler's manner declines, they go (禮貌衰而去). Kong Anguo in He Yan answers with the words of 10.18, 色斯舉也 (the text there: 色斯舉矣 'at a look, up it rose').

sentences.t: 其次辟言。
sentences.l: The next avoid a word.
sentences.i: Those next, from a word.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: when there are words at odds with them, then they go (有違言而後去也); Kong Anguo in He Yan: when there are harsh words, they leave. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: though the four are spoken of in order from great to small, there is no better or worse among them; it is only that what each man met was different (所遇不同耳).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
作者七人矣。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Those who have risen and gone are seven men now.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There are seven men now who have got up and gone.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi treats this as a chapter of its own: the transcription has lost the ○ that should stand before it, but he comments on it separately, quoting a Mr Li (李氏): 作 is 'to rise' — those who have risen and gone off into hiding are now seven; who they were cannot be known, and to insist on finding names to fill the number is forcing it (必求其人以實之則鑿矣). Bao Xian in He Yan reads 作 as 為 'to do (this)', and names the seven: Changju and Jieni, the old man with the basket, the gatekeeper of Shimen, the basket-carrier (14.41–42 here), the border warden of Yi (3.24) and the madman of Chu, Jieyu (長沮桀溺丈人石門荷簣儀封人楚狂接與, the print's 與 for 輿).

sentences.t:
子路宿於石門。
晨門曰：「奚自？」
子路曰：「自孔氏。」
曰：「是知其不可而為之者與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)

sentences.l:
Zilu lodged for the night at Shimen.
The morning gatekeeper said: “From where?”
Zilu said: “From the Kong house.”
He said: “Is this the one who knows it is impossible and yet sets about it?”
sentences.i: Zilu spent a night at Shimen. The keeper of the gate, opening it at dawn, asked him: “Where are you from?” “From Master Kong's,” said Zilu. “Is that the man who knows the thing cannot succeed and works at it regardless?”
sentences.n: 宿 sù 'to lodge for the night'. 石門 Shimen, 'Stone Gate', is a place name (Zhu Xi: 地名). 晨門 is the man in charge of opening the gate at dawn (Zhu Xi: 掌晨啟門); Zhu Xi thinks him probably a worthy man hidden in the post of gate-warden (葢賢人隠於抱関者也). He Yan: the 晨門 is a gatekeeper (閽人). 奚自 'from where?': the question word 奚 comes before 自 'from' (Zhu Xi: 自，従也 — asking where he had come from). 孔氏 'the Kong house', the Master and his household (as 管氏, 3.22). 是…者與 'is this the one who…?' (與 yú; Zhu Xi: 與平聲). Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: the gatekeeper knew the age could not be set right and so did nothing, and with this he mocked Kongzi; but he did not know that for the sage there is no time when the world cannot be worked on. Bao Xian in He Yan: Kongzi knows the age cannot be set right and forces himself to try. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子路宿於石門石門晨門曰, with 石門 twice — most likely a doubled copying ('the Shimen gatekeeper').

sentences.t:
子擊磬於衛。
有荷蕢而過孔氏之門者，
曰：「
有心哉，擊磬乎！」

morph.gloss: clan, house (the family name as a lineage)

sentences.l:
The Master was striking the chime-stones in Wei.
There was one shouldering a straw basket and passing the gate of the Kong house, who said:
“There is heart in it — the striking of the chime-stones!”
sentences.i: The Master was playing the chime-stones in Wei. A man with a straw basket on his shoulder, going past the Master's gate, said: “There is something on his mind, the one who strikes those stones!”
sentences.n: 磬 qìng is a musical instrument (Zhu Xi: 樂器), a set of shaped stones hung on a frame and struck. 擊 jī 'to strike'. 荷 is hè 'to carry on the shoulder' (Zhu Xi: 荷去聲; 荷，擔也); 蕢 kuì a straw basket (草器也). 有…者 'there was one who…', with the whole description between. 有心哉，擊磬乎 'there is heart (in it), the striking of the chime-stones!' — the exclamation first, its subject after. Zhu Xi: the basket-carrier too was a recluse; the sage's heart never forgot the world, and this man heard it in the sound of the stones — so he was no ordinary man. He Yan's comment: 'having heart' means anxious and troubled (契契然). Variants: He Yan's text reads 荷簣 for 荷蕢 (簣 is usually 'a basket for carrying earth', but He Yan's comment glosses it 草器 'a straw basket', as Zhu Xi glosses 蕢, so the difference may be only in the graph), and 孔子之門 'Kongzi's gate' for 孔氏之門.

sentences.t:
既而曰：「
鄙哉，
硜硜乎！
莫己知也，
斯已而已矣。
深則厲，
淺則掲。」

morph.gloss: the sound of a small hard stone (13.20
the sound of a small hard stone (13.20

sentences.l:
When it was done he said: “Crude indeed,
clinking hard like pebbles!
No one knows him —
then let him stop, and that is all.
Deep, then wade in your clothes;
shallow, then hitch them up.”
sentences.i: Then he went on: “How narrow — that hard little clink, clink! If nobody knows him, he should leave off, and there's an end of it. Deep water, wade through in your clothes; shallow water, lift them up.”
sentences.n: The print has 莫已知, a misprint for 莫己知, corrected here. Zhu Xi's own sound note says so: 'the 已 of 莫已 is read like 紀, the others like 以' (莫已之已音紀餘音以) — it is 己 jǐ 'himself, him', and the two 已 of 斯已而已矣 are yǐ 'to stop'; Ruan Yuan's 1816 text prints 己. 既而 'when it was done, after a while'. 鄙 'crude, mean'. 硜硜 kēng kēng (13.20): Zhu Xi — the sound of stone, and also the sense of being single-minded and unbending (專確). 莫己知 is 莫知己 'no one knows him', 己 drawn before the verb after 莫. 斯已而已矣 'then (he should) stop, and that is all'. The last two lines are from the Ode 匏有苦葉 in the Airs of Wei (衛風; Zhu Xi): to go through the water in one's clothes is 厲 lì, to hold up one's clothes and wade is 掲 qì (以衣渉水曰厲，攝衣涉水曰掲; 掲起例反). Zhu Xi: he mocks Kongzi for not stopping when men do not know him, and for not being able to suit himself to the depth of the water. He Yan's comment: this hard clinking is merely trusting in himself, and is of no use; Bao Xian: one should go along with the age as one meets it — in water one must get across somehow; knowing it cannot be done, one should not do it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
果哉！
末之難矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Resolute indeed!
There is nothing hard about it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “He has made up his mind, that one! And if that were all, nothing would be hard.”
sentences.n: 果 'resolute, carried through' (13.20 行必果). Zhu Xi: 'resolute indeed' sighs at how resolute the man is in forgetting the world; 末 is 'none, nothing' (末，無也). The sage's heart is one with Heaven and Earth: he sees all under Heaven as one family and the Central States as one man, and cannot forget them for a single day; so, hearing the basket-carrier, he sighed at his resolve to forget the world, and said that if a man's going out to serve or staying at home were only like this, there would be nothing hard in it (人之出處若但如此則亦無所難矣). He Yan's comment: the man mocked him without knowing his aims, and that is what makes him 'resolute'; and there is no answering him, since he cannot understand the Master's Way. Variant: He Yan's text prints 未之難矣 'not yet hard'; but its comment, which also prints 未, glosses the word 無 'none' (未無也) — Zhu Xi's gloss of 末 — so 未 is most likely a slip for 末 in both places.

sentences.t:
子張曰：「《書》云：『
髙宗諒隂，
三年不言。』
何謂也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zizhang said: “The Documents tell us that Gaozong, in mourning, kept silent for three years. What does that mean?”
sentences.n: 《書》 the Documents (2.21). 髙宗 Gaozong ('High Ancestor', a temple name; 髙 is the edition's form of 高) is King Wuding of Shang (Zhu Xi: 商王武丁也; Kong Anguo in He Yan: the king who restored Yin). 諒隂 is read liáng ān by tradition; Zhu Xi says only that it is the name for the Son of Heaven's dwelling in mourning, and that its sense is not clear (天子居喪之名未詳其義). Kong Anguo takes it word by word: 諒 'truly', 隂 'silent' (諒信也，隂猶黙也) — 'truly silent, he did not speak for three years'. 何謂也 'what is meant (by it)?'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
何必髙宗？
古之人皆然。
君薨，
百官總己以聽於冢宰三年。」

morph.gloss: to take as chief, to look up to as head (Zhu Xi: 主)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Why only Gaozong?
The people of old were all so.
The lord having died,
the hundred offices gathered up their own charges and took orders from the Chief Steward for three years.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Why Gaozong in particular? All the men of old did it. When a ruler died, every officer took his own duties in hand and looked to the Chief Steward for orders for three years.”
sentences.n: The print has 總已, a misprint for 總己, corrected here. Zhu Xi's comment reads 總己 and explains it: each gathered up and held his own office (總己謂總攝己職); Ruan Yuan's 1816 text prints 己. 何必 'why necessarily…?'. 薨 hōng is the death of a lord. Zhu Xi: saying 君 'the lord' means that the feudal lords did so too, not the king alone (言君薨則諸侯亦然). 冢宰 zhǒng zǎi is the Chief Steward (Zhu Xi: 冢宰大宰也, the Grand Steward of 9.6; Kong Anguo in He Yan: the Heaven officer who helps the king govern); since the hundred officers took orders from him, the lord could go three years without speaking. Kong Anguo: when the three years of mourning were over, the king took up the hearing of government himself. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: ranks differ in honour, but all are born of father and mother alike, so the three years' mourning runs from the Son of Heaven to the common people; Zizhang did not doubt that — he probably feared that if a ruler did not speak for three years his ministers would have nowhere to take their orders, and disorder might rise from it; Kongzi told him they took orders from the Chief Steward, so disorder was not to be feared.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
上好禮，
則民易使也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If those above love the rites,
then the people are easy to employ.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When those at the top love the rites, the people are easily led.”
sentences.n: 上好禮 'those above love the rites' as 13.4. 好 is hào 'to love', 易 yì 'easy' (Zhu Xi: 好易皆去聲). 易使 'easy to employ': the verb after the adjective is taken passively, as 13.25 易事. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: when the rites reach everywhere, each man's lot is settled, so the people are easy to employ (禮達而分定故民易使). He Yan's comment: none of the people dare be irreverent, so they are easy to employ.

sentences.t:
子路問君子。
子曰：「脩己以敬。」
曰：「如斯而已乎？」
曰：「脩己以安人。」
曰：「如斯而已乎？」
曰：「脩己以安百姓。
脩己以安百姓，
堯舜其猶病諸！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
surname, clan name (同姓 'the same surname', Zhu Xi: 禮不娶同姓, 'the rites do not take a wife of one's own surname')
surname, clan name (同姓 'the same surname', Zhu Xi: 禮不娶同姓, 'the rites do not take a wife of one's own surname')

sentences.l:
Zilu asked about the gentleman.
The Master said: “He cultivates himself with reverence.”
He said: “Like this, and that is all?”
He said: “He cultivates himself so as to give peace to others.”
He said: “Like this, and that is all?”
He said: “He cultivates himself so as to give peace to the hundred clans.
Cultivating oneself so as to give peace to the hundred clans —
even Yao and Shun still felt themselves short in this.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked about the gentleman. The Master said: “He cultivates himself and is reverent.” “Is that all?” “He cultivates himself and so brings peace to those around him.” “Is that all?” “He cultivates himself and so brings peace to the whole people. To cultivate oneself and so bring peace to the whole people — even Yao and Shun felt they fell short in this.”
sentences.n: 脩 xiū (= 修) 'to put in order, to cultivate'. 以 first 'with, in' (脩己以敬), then 'so as to' (以安人). 如斯而已乎 'like this, and that is all?' — 而已 'and stop there'. 百姓 'the hundred clans', the whole people (12.9). The last line is 6.28's, with its English. Zhu Xi: 'cultivating oneself with reverence' — the Master's words were complete and exhaustive, but Zilu thought them too little, so he told him twice more of how this, filled out and full, reaches others of itself; there is no other way. 人 is said against oneself; 百姓 takes in all men. That Yao and Shun still felt short means nothing can be added beyond this — so as to check Zilu and make him turn back and look for it close at hand. The sage's heart has no limit: however well the age is governed, how could he be sure that within the four seas not one thing failed of its place? He quotes Master Cheng: 'the gentleman cultivates himself so as to give peace to the hundred clans; earnest and reverent, and the world is at peace' (篤恭而天下平, the Doctrine of the Mean). Kong Anguo in He Yan: 人 means friends and the nine degrees of kin; 病 is 'to find it hard' (病猶難也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 脩己以敬人 'cultivates himself so as to respect others' (its print writes 巳 for 己), but Kong Anguo's comment there, 'to be reverent in his person' (敬其身也), fits Zhu Xi's text.

sentences.t:
原壤夷俟。
子曰：「
幼而不孫弟，
長而無述焉；
老而不死：是為賊。」
以杖叩其脛。

morph.gloss: Rang, in the name 原壤 (14.46)

sentences.i: Yuan Rang sat waiting on his haunches. The Master said: “Not humble or respectful as a boy, nothing worth telling as a man, and now old and still not dead — you do nothing but harm.” And he rapped him on the shin with his staff.
sentences.n: 原壤 Yuan Rang was an old friend of Kongzi's; Zhu Xi recalls that when his mother died he sang, and calls him probably one of Laozi's sort who set themselves outside the rites (葢老氏之流自放於禮法之外者). 夷 is to squat (Zhu Xi: 夷，蹲踞也; Ma Rong in He Yan: 踞也), 俟 'to wait': seeing Kongzi coming, he squatted and waited for him. 孫 xùn = 遜 'humble' and 弟 tì 'deferential' (Zhu Xi: 孫弟並去聲); 幼 yòu 'young'; 長 zhǎng 'grown up' (上聲). 述 'to be told of', Zhu Xi 猶稱也 'to be praised'. 賊 'a despoiler' — Zhu Xi: the name for one who harms others; from youth to age he had shown no single good thing, and living on long in the world he served only to spoil custom and disorder ways. 叩 kòu 'to knock' (Zhu Xi: 叩音口, i.e. kǒu; modern kòu; Kong Anguo: 叩，擊也), 脛 jìng 'the shin' (其定反; 足骨也). Zhu Xi: having rebuked him, Kongzi gave his shin a light tap with the staff he was trailing, as if to make him stop squatting.

sentences.t:
闕黨童子將命。
或問之曰：「益者與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
A boy of Que village carried messages.
Someone asked about him, saying: “One who is making progress?”
sentences.i: A boy from the village of Que was carrying messages for the Master. Someone asked about him: “Is he coming on well?”
sentences.n: 闕黨 Que is the name of a 黨, a village community (Zhu Xi: 黨名). 童子 'a boy': Zhu Xi, one not yet capped (未冠者之稱), as 7.28. 將命 'to carry the charge', passing words between host and guest (Zhu Xi: 傳賓主之言; Ma Rong in He Yan, taking them in and out); 將 is jiāng. 益者與 'one who is advancing?' (與 yú; Zhu Xi: 與平聲): Zhu Xi, the questioner supposed the boy had made progress in his learning, so that Kongzi had him carry messages as a mark of favour. Variant: He Yan's text reads 闕黨童子將命矣, adding 矣.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾見其居於位也，
見其與先生並行也：
非求益者也，
欲速成者也。」

morph.gloss: to grow, to be born, to arise

sentences.l:
The Master said: “I see him sitting in a place,
see him walking side by side with his elders:
he is not one seeking to make progress;
he is one wanting to be grown quickly.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I see him take his seat among the grown men, and walk abreast of his elders. He is not after progress; he wants to be grown up in a hurry.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: by the rites a boy should sit in a corner and walk behind (禮童子當隅坐隨行); Kongzi says he sees this boy not keeping to the rule — he does not seek to advance, he only wants to be grown quickly. So the Master gave him the errands to run, to watch the order of elder and younger and practise the manners of bowing and giving way: it was to check and teach him, not to favour and single him out. 居於位 'to sit in a place': He Yan's comment — a boy sits in a corner and has no place; only grown men have one. 先生 'the elders' (2.8; Bao Xian in He Yan: 先生，成人也 'grown men'). 並 bìng 'side by side'; 與 yǔ 'with'. Bao Xian: walking abreast, not falling behind, is against the rites; such a one wants to be grown quickly and is not seeking to advance. Variant: He Yan's text reads 吾見其踞於位也 'I see him squatting in a place'; its own comment speaks only of the boy's having no place, so 踞 may be a slip for 居.
